list.listitem: Hantaviruses are a group of negative sense RNA viruses, each virus associated with a specific rodent reservoir. C

There are two main clinical syndromes: hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) and hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), the former encountered throughout the Americas and the latter in Asia and Europe. C
Diagnosis is primarily clinical: hantavirus infection should be considered in patients with fever and thrombocytopenia with the appropriate exposure history. C
The clinical hallmark of HCPS is severe pulmonary vascular permeability with severe cardiac dysfunction. Intensive care support is the mainstay of therapy. C

background.definition: Hantaviruses are a genus (Orthohantavirus) of viruses in the Bunyaviridae family. Each virus is associated with a specific rodent species that causes hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) or hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS). They are named after the Hantan River in South Korea.

list.listitem: From 1993 through 2021 there were 850 cases of hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) identified in the United States of which all but 29 were HCPS.
The majority of the cases (44%) originated from exposure in New Mexico, California, Colorado, and Arizona. Overall, 27 other states have also reported cases of HCPS.
An outbreak of HFRS occurred in several states caused by the Seoul virus transmitted by pet rats (Rattus norvegicus).
Hantaviruses are enveloped, negative-sense, single-stranded RNA viruses.
Hantaviruses cause two different clinical syndromes: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS).
Each hantavirus is associated with a specific rodent reservoir. The two main rodent reservoir subfamilies are Murinae and Sigmodontinae (see ).
The Murinae subfamily are the reservoirs for viruses that cause HFRS.
The Sigmodontinae subfamily are the reservoirs for Sin Nombre, Black Creek Canal, Bayou, New York, and Andes viruses, which are associated with HCPS.
The Sin Nombre virus is the most common cause of HCPS in North America and is transmitted by the deer mouse, Peromyscus maniculatus.
A systematic review concluded that there was no evidence for human to human transmission.
Human disease begins by a process of inhalation of an aerosol that contains the infectious virus.
A competent cellular immune response, primarily by CD8+ T cells, is needed for clearance of the virus. Hantavirus-specific T cell response has been associated with disease severity.
Hantaviruses are not highly cytopathic in cell culture.
The clinical manifestations of HCPS and HFRS are thought to be induced by cytokines.

Prevention is primarily related to minimizing rodent-human contact. This can include rodent-proofing of homes, reduction of rodent cover around houses, minimization of food available to rodents, trapping rodents in and around dwellings, and careful disposal of dead rodents. C
A Chinese vaccine has been developed and approximately 2 million doses are administered annually. Numerous other vaccine trials are underway.
Diagnosis depends on high clinical suspicion in patients with fever and thrombocytopenia particularly if disease arises in a rural setting. C
Confirm the diagnosis with serologic testing. C

list.listitem: Suspect hantavirus infection in patients with fever and thrombocytopenia who may have had exposure to rodents.
There are two clinical syndromes caused by hantaviruses. Both can be severe or mild depending on the specific infecting virus ().

HCPS is defined by cardiopulmonary dysfunction ranging from mild hypoxemia with stable hemodynamics to rapidly progressive respiratory failure with cardiogenic shock (). Predominant clinical manifestations include fever, thrombocytopenia, elevated lactic dehydrogenase, pulmonary edema from marked pulmonary vascular permeability, and cardiogenic shock. This generally develops in a healthy person who lives in a rural setting. The vast number of HCPS cases are sporadic, i.e., not associated with outbreaks.

HFRS is defined by a febrile phase lasting 3 days to 5 days, followed by a hypotensive phase with thrombocytopenia and disseminated intravascular coagulation, then an oliguric renal failure phase, and finally a polyuric phase with marked electrolyte imbalance. The predominant clinical manifestations include fever, systemic vascular permeability, hemorrhagic tendencies, proteinuria, and renal failure.
During epidemics with respiratory viruses, HCPS can easily be overlooked. Such was the case in Arizona in 2020 when the emphasis was on detection of COVID 19 infection (PMC10370831)18.
Diagnosis of hantavirus infection is made primarily by clinical suspicion and can be confirmed by serologic testing.

Serologic tests include IgM and IgG Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), which are available from public health departments and the CDC. Acute-phase and convalescent-phase sera should reflect a 4-fold rise in IgG antibody titer (or the presence of IgM in acute-phase sera) to be diagnostic for hantaviral disease.
Looking carefully at the peripheral blood smear can be helpful in early cases; there are often very high leukocyte counts and immunoblasts in the peripheral smear.

Levels of IgG antibodies usually peak during the first week of illness and remain detectable for a long time. There is widespread cross-reactivity between the various hantaviruses, but specificity for any hantavirus is well conserved.
The Sin Nombre viral antigen is primarily used in the United States.
Immunohistochemical staining is useful in establishing retrospective diagnoses from fixed tissue.
Reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (PCR) tests are available to detect viral RNA in blood and tissue samples.
Isolation of hantaviruses in culture is difficult and therefore is not used for diagnosis.
Suspect hantavirus in patients with fever and thrombocytopenia who have risk factors for rodent exposure in an endemic area (this includes travellers to endemic areas).
Order an ELISA test and contact the local health department if you suspect a hantavirus infection.
Treatment is primarily supportive; ribavirin may be effective in patients with HFRS.
The mainstay of treatment is intensive and specialized supportive care. C
RCTs indicate that ribavirin may improve outcomes in HFRS, but not in HCPS. B
RCTs indicate that ribavirin may improve outcomes in HFRS, but not in HCPS.,
An open-label trial of ribavirin failed to show any efficacy in HCPS patients. This was thought to be because death typically occurs within 24 to 48 hours of hospitalization.
Cardiotonic drugs should be used early because of the decreased cardiac output and increased systemic vascular resistance seen in both HFRS and HCPS.
A Phase 2 clinical trial found no benefit of corticosteroids in the cardiopulmonary phase.
There is no specific treatment or cure of hantavirus infections. The mainstay of treatment is supportive care.
Vascular leak leads to extravasation into retroperitoneal tissues in HFRS or into lung in HCPS. Early management should avoid excessive fluid administration.
Plasma protein, whole blood, or both, may be useful in treating hemorrhage and/or shock.
Patients with HCPS require close monitoring of oxygenation so that timely intubation and mechanical ventilation can be provided, if needed.
Severe HFRS may require hemodialysis during the oliguric phase to treat hyperkalemia, volume overload, and uremia.

During the oliguric phase of HFRS, the two major causes of death are pulmonary edema and intracerebral hemorrhage. During the diuresis stage of HFRS, large volumes of isosthenuric urine leads to potentially fatal volume and electrolyte abnormalities.
Early initiation of extracorporeal membrane oxygenation may decrease complication rates and improve overall survival.
Clinical deterioration can occur rapidly in patients with hantaviral infections; intensive care support and close cardiopulmonary monitoring should be made available in a timely fashion.
Case reports have documented long-term complications from hantavirus infections including renal, neurologic, and cardiac sequelae.
In the United States, 36% of cases have resulted in death. B
Long-term sequelae may exist, but have not been clearly defined. C

feature.caption: Characteristics of Hantavirus CardioPulmonary Syndrome.*
feature.feature_body:
Incubation Period 1-2 weeks
Early signs and symptoms 3-5 days fever, myalgias, malaise. Often with nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. IgM antibody and immunoblasts present in peripheral blood.
Disease Course
Hematologic Thrombocytopenia. Abnormal partial thromboplastin time. Clinical bleeding diathesis uncommon.
Endothelial permeability Pulmonary edema leading to dyspnea and hypoxemia.
Hemodynamic instability Hypotension and shock.
Fever Some continue to have fever.
Hemodynamic recovery Shock improves in 3-6 days.
Renal failure Proteinuria is common. Approximately 20% have serum creatinine >2.0 mg/dL.
Duration of illness Improvement in pulmonary edema leads to rapid recovery.
Diuresis Diuresis of resorbed fluid.
Mortality 30%-40% of patients die 24-48 hours after admission.
*Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome caused by Sin Nombre virus.
